prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and for its first experimental observation with protected edge states in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B055, as a single-part prize. The case is that the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall effect replaced symmetry breaking with the topology of the occupied bands as the organising principle for a class of insulators. It was an original idea, it was realised in HgTe quantum wells within about a year, and it has been confirmed in many independent material families, including InAs/GaSb, Bi-based compounds and the three-dimensional generalisation seen by ARPES. It has also changed everyday electronic-structure practice, since computing topological invariants and screening materials for them is now routine. Two decades of confirmation make it mature in a way twisted bilayer graphene is not yet, and the 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions and Haldane-type models rather than this line. Having read the full exchange I would write the citation narrowly, around the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect, because that is the claim the three supplied names actually cover: Kane and Mele made the prediction and the Z2 classification, and Molenkamp's group made the observation.
statement.case_against: The credit gap has not been closed by the round-1 exchange. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the platform, Fu, Kane and Mele (with Moore, Balents and Roy) made the three-dimensional generalisation, and the ARPES work established it experimentally, and none of these are in the supplied three names. A narrow quantum spin Hall citation shrinks that gap but does not remove it, and a prize that leaves out the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp where to look will be contested. The case also rests on conceptual influence, because the promised dissipationless edge transport has not materialised. By contrast, B015 has a cleaner two-name credit, and five colleagues who prefer it are right that this is a real advantage. I am therefore keeping B055 on its scientific reach, not because its attribution is better, and I regard this as a closer call than my round-1 text suggested.

responses.point: Kroll holds B015 first as a clean invention (Katori) plus decisive realization (Ye) with independent reproduction, and asks whether omitting B006 or pairing the clock with a condensed-matter candidate needs a principled reason.
responses.response: I take the chair's question to us directly: B015 has the cleanest credit on the table and I said in round 1 that I would not oppose it. What I still weigh differently is scientific reach. A lattice clock extends what can be measured, while B055 changed which question one asks about a band structure. On Kroll's two-part idea, I looked at it seriously. With a three-person limit across the whole configuration, pairing B015 (two names) with B055 would leave one name for the topological part, and that cannot be defended given the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp structure. So I do not propose a two-part prize. If the committee chooses B015 alone I would support that outcome, and Kroll's point that the condensed-matter alternatives carry larger attribution problems is correct.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that Katori's magic-wavelength idea rests on genuine atomic-structure insight and that the comb made optical frequencies countable while the lattice clock is what is counted, so B015 is distinct from the 2005 prize; she also flags that single-ion clocks reached comparable uncertainty by another route.
responses.response: This changes my view of B015 more than anything else in the exchange. Magic-wavelength trapping is an electronic-structure argument at heart: choosing a wavelength at which the polarisabilities of two atomic states match is something I can evaluate, and it is a real piece of physics, not engineering. Her distinction between the comb and the clock answers the question I raised in round 1 about the 2005 overlap. Her ion-clock caveat is the one I think matters, because a citation worded around neutral-atom lattices would be silent about the ion route. That is acceptable only if the citation names the lattice concept explicitly and does not claim to honour optical clocks generally. This is why I moved B015 to the front of my alternatives.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B006 first, argues that the discovery of the phases does not depend on the superconducting mechanism, that B006 has a cleaner division of labour between prediction and experiment than B055, and that he could move to B055 if maturity outweighs novelty.
responses.response: I accept the logic that the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in magic-angle graphene stands independent of the mechanism, and I agree the prediction followed by surprise structure is the strongest feature of B006. We disagree on timing. About eight years in, the community cannot yet say whether the superconductivity is conventional, and sample and twist-angle dependence still limits comparison between groups, so a citation would have to describe what was seen, not what it means. B055 is on the other side of that line. I also still think the B006 credit is less clean than he suggests, because early continuum-model work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto precedes Bistritzer and MacDonald. I keep B006 as my second alternative and would revisit it in a later cycle.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B023 to B015, argues it is original, decisive and independently reproduced with a two-person credit, and concedes the novelty risk against the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes and the chance that the committee would want ion and lattice clocks treated together.
responses.response: I think Mehlig puts the two real tests correctly: novelty against 2005 and 2012, and the possibility that treating ion and lattice clocks together reopens the credit. On the first, I would accept a citation that says 'optical lattice clocks' explicitly and does not mention frequency standards in general, since the magic-wavelength lattice with many neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime is the new element. On the second, I do not think the principled line between inventor and refiner is hard to draw on the supplied evidence: Katori supplied the concept and Ye the performance level and the many-body control, while Ludlow, Lemke and the Paris and PTB groups reproduced or refined at comparable levels. That is the same line I would draw for B055, and it is the reason I regard Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang as an actual omission there and not a refinement.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B024 and argues that circuit QED is distinct from the 2025 single-circuit tunnelling prize, and that the argument for waiting is weak on the science.
responses.response: Johansson answered my round-1 objection reasonably: coupling circuits to photons and the readout architecture are physically distinct from macroscopic tunnelling in a single circuit. I still think the committee must be able to state why a second superconducting-circuit prize within a year is justified, and Girvin's role in both the proposal and the transmon leaves a real gap among Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf. I did not move B024 into my alternatives, and the open recusal question should be settled by him and the chair before B024 is weighed, though I record that I do not think it decides the science.

uncertainties: Whether a narrowly framed quantum spin Hall citation is accepted by the committee as defensible without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, or whether the omission is judged decisive against B055.
Whether the redefinition of the SI second should be completed before B015, and whether B015 would then be the stronger configuration; I regard it as a supporting consideration, not a precondition.
Whether the choice between B055 and B015 should turn on scientific reach or on cleanness of credit, which I cannot settle from the supplied evidence alone.
Whether B006 will be judged mature enough in a later cycle, given the unresolved mechanism of superconductivity and correlated states.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My work in electronic-structure theory and magnetism uses methods related to topological-materials calculations, but my profile documents no personal or institutional connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye, or the other credited names on the shortlist. I have no new disclosure since round 1.
